text: Mid-course test, Track 2. Good afternoon. I'm joined today by Climate Change Author Rachel Greenaker. We're talking about planting trees. Why trees? Hello, Jeremy. Trees use the carbon dioxide that we humans produce, which is the main gas heating the planet and causing global warming. Many people, may included, see planting more trees as one possible solution to the problem of climate change. Right. I understand the government in an effort to support green initiatives has promised to plant millions of trees per year. That's quite a large number. You are right that the government is supporting green initiatives, but the number of trees they want to plant, around 30 million, is in fact lower than other countries which have programs in place to plant billions. Why is this such a popular idea? Well, in addition to looking beautiful, forests have practical benefits. They support wildlife, of course, and hold back flood water. This is especially important with the increasing storms we are experiencing as a result of global warming. What's more, trees provide wood, which has a broad range of uses from building and construction materials to paper and oils used in paints. As I already mentioned, trees help clean the air by absorbing carbon dioxide. They take in around 20 million tons of carbon dioxide per year when we include the additional 30 million trees the government has promised to plant. This sounds good on paper, but I imagine the decision isn't popular with everyone. No, there are problems, Jeremy. There's the question of where to plant a new forest. If they planted where crops are grown or where animals are being raised, then some sort of payment would be necessary for the farmer who owns the land. It could take decades before the farmer might expect to make any sort of profit from a new forest. Then there's the problem of planting. I have watched experienced tree planters planting trees at a rate of 1 every 4 seconds, which equals around 3 to 4,000 trees a day. They are actually more efficient than the machines that can do the same job. Unfortunately, it isn't a popular job in this country, so finding labour might be difficult, unless we employ experts from overseas, are those the only challenges? No. As I mentioned earlier, trees grow slowly, but not only that, young trees or saplings require lots of care. They are affected by extreme changes in the weather, diseases and insects, many die before they reach maturity. This brings me to another issue. Trees can only use significant amounts of carbon dioxide once they reach the age of around 30 years, so the benefits to the environment are not going to happen quickly. I said before we can use trees for wood, but if a tree dies and is left in the ground, all the carbon the tree absorbed when it was alive is released back into the earth and therefore the atmosphere. What can we do about those issues? The key to success is good land management, so the young trees have the best possible chance of surviving until they reach maturity. Let me tell you more about how we can help young trees to reach the age of 30 years. For instance, we can attach instruments to tree trunks, which measure how fast the tree is growing and how healthy it is. We can also make sure we plant more than one species of tree. This means that if one species were lost because of a specific disease, the other might survive. Also, we should not forget trees require water and some species more than others. While a newly planted forest might protect one local community from flooding, it might leave a neighbouring community without enough drinking water. We must remember this is a long-term plan, so we need long-term goals, otherwise we're going to fail. Very interesting, Rachel. We must stop there, I'm afraid, as we're out of time. Thank you for joining us today.
